implementation_notes: kotlinx.serialization models JSON as data: JsonObject implements Map<String, JsonElement>, so the projection is literally filterKeys over the encoded resource, with the value types still handled by the serializer. Unknown names are validated against a selectable set first. Use this for generic or heterogeneous boundaries; when the shape is fixed, the typed view-data-class variant is cheaper and self-documenting.
pitfalls: filterKeys only filters the top level - nested selections need recursion into JsonObject/JsonArray, otherwise a selected sub-object still carries everything.

The Json configuration decides the empty-value story: encodeDefaults/explicitNulls change whether a projected-but-empty field serializes as null or disappears, so pin the Json instance at the boundary.
Encoding to JsonElement builds the complete tree before filtering; on hot paths serialise straight to the wire with a serializer per view instead.

variants.name: Per-view @Serializable data classes
variants.idiom_name: explicit view data classes (UserCard/UserFull) selected by an allowlisted view name
variants.implementation_notes: With a fixed set of published views the projection is a type: one @Serializable data class per view, and the boundary maps the requested selection onto the view catalog. The compiler pins the shape, serialization is allocation-light, and adding a field to the entity cannot leak it into an existing view. This trades the flexibility of arbitrary masks for a contract that is impossible to get wrong at runtime.
pitfalls: Data-class copy() is shallow: a view property holding a MutableList still shares (and can leak) the underlying elements, so nested collections must be defensively copied or wrapped read-only.
Every new field combination needs code; without a bounded catalog the when() branches grow combinatorially.
Because the views are ordinary data classes they are easy to reuse as input DTOs - keep input and output types apart or clients will start sending projected shapes back.
